what_it_does: Modern chips connect their many cores through an on-chip communication fabric called a Network-on-Chip (NoC) — essentially a tiny internet inside the chip that routes data between processing units. When many cores send data simultaneously, subtle timing interactions can create security holes that are extremely hard to find by hand. InterConFuzz is an automated testing tool that hunts for these bugs by throwing millions of carefully crafted, semi-random data packets at the NoC design and using a technique called symbolic execution (which reasons mathematically about all the paths a packet could take) to make sure the randomized tests actually reach hard-to-trigger corner cases. It plugs into the standard chip-verification workflow that designers already use (called UVM, a structured simulation environment), so teams can adopt it without rebuilding their test infrastructure. The key claim is that it finds security flaws that traditional checklist-style tests miss.
